text: Linearisability is essentially the illusion of a single copy of data. We build distributed systems hoping to maintain that illusion, but physics and the speed of light violently disagree.
context: Linearisability is the gold standard for concurrent object correctness: every operation appears to take effect instantaneously at some point between its invocation and completion, consistent with a sequential history. The CAP theorem formalises a fundamental tradeoff: under network partition, a distributed system cannot simultaneously be consistent and available. Weaker consistency models—eventual consistency, causal consistency, session guarantees—each relax linearisability in different ways to recover availability or performance, but none can be composed with the same algebraic simplicity as sequential code. The unresolved tension is that most distributed systems documentation describes which model is used, but not the class of application-level bugs that become possible when programmers assume a stronger model than the system provides.

The unresolved tension is that most distributed systems documentation describes which model is used, but not the class of application-level bugs that become possible when programmers assume a stronger model than the system provides.
